newsitem.title: PAKISTAN: Five killed in Afghan air raid on rebel-held city.
newsitem.headline: Five killed in Afghan air raid on rebel-held city.

text.p: Afghan government jets bombed targets in the eastern city of Jalalabad, now held by Taleban militia rebels, on Sunday, killing five people and wounding a score of civilians, Taleban and U.N. sources in Pakistan said.

The sources said the planes attacked the airport, the governor's palace and the nearby Spinghar Hotel from about 7.45 a.m. (0315 GMT). They also dropped anti-personnel mines near the Behsud Bridge, about two km (one mile) west of the city.
A Taleban official in the Pakistani border city of Peshawar said five people had been killed in the raid.

Daniel Bellamy, chief of mission for the U.N. High Commissioner for Refugees, said at least 25 civilian casualties had been admitted at one hospital in the city, captured in a swift advance by the Islamic Taleban militia on Wednesday.
"The raids and anti-aircraft fire created panic in the city," Bellamy told Reuters in Islamabad.
"The streets are deserted and people are sheltering at home," he said, citing reports from U.N. staff on the spot.
Bellamy said eight U.N. international staff were in Jalalabad, but might be evacuated if conditions deteriorated.
The Pakistan-based Afghan Islamic Press (AIP) said the raid had damaged the ornate Bagh-i-Shahi palace built by 19th-century Afghan ruler Amir Abdur Rahman beside the Kabul river.
The building's most recent occupant was former provincial governor Haji Abdul Qadir, leader of a group of neutral factions that had previously controlled Nangarhar province.

The Taleban's capture of Jalalabad, astride the main Kabul-Pakistan highway, dealt a major blow to the Kabul government. The rebels are fighting to oust President Burhanuddin Rabbani and install a strict Islamic order.

The latest Taleban success has given some respite to the battered Afghani currency, which rose to about 13,000 to the dollar on Sunday from about 19,000 before Jalalabad fell, currency dealers in Peshawar said.
Many Afghan traders support the Taleban, hoping that a rebel takeover would reopen roads throughout Afghanistan.
Afghan sources in Pakistan said on Saturday that government forces had checked the Taleban advance towards the strategic town of Sarobi, about 60 km (37 miles) east of Kabul.
A Taleban leader in Jalalabad, Mullah Muhammad Rabbani, said on Sunday he expected Kunar province, northeast of Jalalabad, to fall to his forces soon as a result of talks with local leaders.
He told AIP that a pro-government faction led by Maulvi Samiullah had agreed in talks on Saturday to let the Taleban take control of the province without a fight.
He said a government commander named Hazrat Ali was understood to be ready to withdraw his forces to Sarobi or Kabul under the deal, rather than confront the Taleban.
No comment from the government side was immediately available.
